title: Dashboard chronicle fragmenter: seek-accelerator for long-range timeline queries
creator: Carlos Mendes
description:
Problem: Long-range timeline queries (e.g., tenant activity over 30–90 days) are a major source of p95/p99 tail latency in the Console. Existing pagination is offset/anchor based and frequently requires scanning large time ranges or merging many shards, which leads to expensive DB work and unpredictable latency under tenant hotspots.

Goal: Implement a server-side "chronicle fragmenter" and seek-accelerator protocol so dashboard query APIs serve long-range timeline pages with consistent p50/p95 latency and lower IO cost. The approach should integrate with the usage analytics streaming pipeline to populate a lightweight per-tenant fragment index and a small hot-fragment micro-cache at the API edge.

High-level approach: 
- Materialize chronological fragments: a nearline job (streaming pipeline) writes fixed-time-range fragments (e.g., daily/6-hour slices) into a columnar object store with small summary metadata for each fragment (min/max timestamp, event count, top-entities).
- Per-tenant fragment index: a compact index (fragment_id, time_span, estimated_cost, popularity_score) stored in Redis/mini-KV for fast lookup and used by the query router to choose fragments to fetch.
- Seek-accelerator tokens: replace long opaque cursors with stateless tokens that encode fragment_id + local offset + optional prefetch hint. This keeps the API stateless while enabling targeted seeks into the right fragment. Tokens are HMAC-signed for integrity.
- Edge micro-cache: API layer caches hot fragments (recent or high-popularity) in LRU with TTL. Cache invalidation via streaming invalidation events from pipeline when fragment materialization changes.
- Merge strategy: query engine merges at fragment granularity using the columnar fragment summaries and only reads rows for fragments that match the requested time range; for large windows we fetch summaries first and stream fragments in parallel with backpressure/hedging controls.

Acceptance criteria (measurable):
- P50 latency for 30-day timeline queries reduced by >=25% compared to baseline (measured on tenant sample set).
- P95 latency reduced by >=35%.
- API cost (DB read amplification) for long-range queries reduced by >=40% measured by average read bytes per request.
- Rolling canary shows no error rate increase at the API surface or in downstream analytics jobs.

Instrumentation & metrics to add:
- fragment_lookup_latency_ms, fragment_fetch_bytes, fragment_fetch_latency_ms, seek_token_decode_errors, edge_fragment_hit_rate, merge_stream_backpressure_seconds.
- Dashboard panels: per-tenant fragment hit-rate, 95th latency delta vs baseline, per-tenant read-bytes/request.

Design doc & artifacts:
- Design spec: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Chronicle+Fragmenter+Design (draft)
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/7894 (edge + token plumbing)
- Streaming job harness branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/analytics/pull/202 (fragment materialization prototype)

Implementation plan (phases):
1) Prototype: implement stateless seek token and server decode path; wire small in-memory fragment index for experiments (1 sprint).
2) Pipeline integration: add fragment materializer job to streaming pipeline and publish fragment manifests to KV (2 sprints).
3) API edge cache + merge engine: implement edge micro-cache with invalidation and fragment-based merge strategy (2 sprints).
4) Rollout & canary: rollout to 5% tenants -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback on latency/regressions (1 sprint).

Trade-offs and risks: 
- Increased storage footprint: materialized fragments duplicate some analytic data, though columnar compression mitigates cost. We estimate 10–18% extra storage for fragments for our sampled workloads.
- Fragment staleness: nearline materialization introduces a small lag (tunable, currently targeting <2 minutes). Interactive workloads must still be served by the real-time path for the freshest events; fragment path is optimized for historical scans.
- Complexity in invalidation: we must ensure the invalidation stream is reliable; fallback is conservative TTL-based eviction.
- Edge cache memory pressure: need size limits and eviction policies per-region/tenant.

Rollout plan and safety gates:
- Canary metric set: p50/p95 latency, error rate, fragment_decode_errors, increased DB read bytes.
- Start with low-traffic tenants and opt-in customers (internal Beta).
- Automated rollback triggers: >10% increase in p95 vs baseline on canary cohort, or >0.5% absolute API error rate increase.
- Post-mortem and metrics review after 72 hours of stable canary.

Testing:
- Unit tests for token encoding/decoding (including tamper tests).
- Integration tests that simulate fragment manifests and verify merge correctness across time boundaries.
- Load test using replayed telemetry traces (30-day heavy tenants) comparing baseline vs fragment path.

Open implementation decisions (to resolve in design review):
- Fragment duration: daily vs 6-hour windows vs adaptive durations based on tenant activity. (Default: 6-hour to balance file sizes and seek cost).
- Index placement: Redis vs RocksDB-on-SSD per-region. Redis chosen for low-latency but increases memory cost; alternative is a tiered approach.
- Token format: currently HMAC(salt|fragment_id|offset|hint|expiry) using existing signing keys; consider encrypting payload for privacy.

Security & compliance notes: tokens include fragment identifiers but no raw event data. Tokens will be HMAC-signed and expire after a configurable TTL. Follow-up: run a brief threat model with Security for token forgery and replay risk.

Owners & reviewers:
- Owner: Priya Kaur (backend)
- Analytics pipeline owner: Samir Patel
- Performance reviewer: Lena Ortega

Expected timeline: 6–8 weeks from prototype to full rollout assuming no major blockers.

Follow-ups after rollout:
- Evaluate moving to adaptive fragment sizing per-tenant based on activity heatmaps.
- Consider cross-tenant deduplication of low-cardinality fragments to reduce storage.
